finding.summary: According to Tax Policy Center modeling reported by Vox, about half of U.S. tax units paid more than $750 in federal individual income tax in both 2016 and 2017. A tax unit can be an individual or a married couple, with dependents, and includes people whose income was too low to require filing. Separately, the Congressional Research Service estimated that 44% of U.S. households would pay no federal income tax in 2016. The comparison therefore applies to many taxpayers, but whether a particular listener paid more cannot be determined without their tax information.

finding.question: What did Donald Trump actually say about being smart and using the tax system when his taxes were raised, and in what context did he say it?
finding.summary: During the September 26, 2016 presidential debate, Hillary Clinton suggested Trump had paid no federal income tax in years covered by records submitted for a casino license. Trump interjected, “That makes me smart.” Neither “Because I’m smart” nor “I know how to game the system” was his wording in that exchange; they paraphrase his remark rather than quote it verbatim. Separately, at an October 3, 2016 rally, Trump said he had legally and “brilliantly” used the tax laws to his benefit.

sources.title: The First Presidential Debate
sources.snippet:
(SOUNDBITE OF 2016 PRESIDENTIAL DEBATE)

CLINTON: Maybe he doesn't want the American people, all of you watching tonight, to know that he's paid nothing in federal taxes because the only years that anybody's ever seen were a couple of years when he had to turn them over to state authorities when he was trying to get a casino license, and they showed he didn't pay any federal income tax. So...

TRUMP: That makes me smart.

report_raw.claim: Why should you pay more taxes than Donald Trump pays? And that’s a fact. $750. Remember what he said when that was raised a while ago, how he only pays … He said, ‘Because I’m smart. I know how to game the system.’
report_raw.justification: The New York Times reported that Trump’s federal income tax was $750 in each of 2016 and 2017; the figure is his income-tax liability, not all taxes paid or necessarily the cash remitted during each year. [S1][S2] Tax Policy Center modeling estimated that about half of U.S. tax units paid more than $750 in federal income tax in those years, but the comparison cannot establish what an unspecified listener paid. [S5] At the 2016 debate, Trump responded “That makes me smart” to an allegation that he had paid no federal income tax in earlier years—not to the later $750 report. [S8] He later said he had “brilliantly” used tax laws to his benefit, but the supplied evidence does not show him saying the exact words attributed to him. [S10] Inference: The tax figure and the substance of Trump’s remarks have a basis, but the claim presents a paraphrase as a direct quotation and conflates the earlier exchange with the $750 report.
key_points: The reported $750 was federal income-tax liability for each of 2016 and 2017, not a measure of all taxes. [S1][S2]
About half of tax units were estimated to have paid more than $750 in federal income tax in those years. [S5]
Trump’s actual debate words were “That makes me smart,” in response to an allegation about earlier tax years. [S8]
Trump separately said he had “brilliantly” used tax laws, but the supplied evidence does not substantiate the claim’s exact quotation. [S10]
report_raw.counter_argument: A case for treating the claim as materially accurate is that $750 was reported for two years, many tax units paid more, and Trump did boast both about being smart and about using tax laws to his benefit. [S1][S5][S8][S10] That does not overcome the claim’s presentation of different words as a direct quotation or its implied link between the debate remark and the later $750 report. [S8]
evidence_gaps: The contemporary $750 reporting relied on tax-return data obtained by the Times; the returns themselves had not been publicly released, and Trump disputed the report.
The supplied evidence does not identify the occasion of the claim or establish what an unspecified listener paid.
A recording or transcript of any other occasion on which Trump allegedly used the exact quoted words could further test the quotation.

evidence_gaps: The contemporary $750 reporting relied on tax-return data obtained by the Times; the returns themselves had not been publicly released, and Trump disputed the report.
The supplied evidence does not identify the occasion of the claim or establish what an unspecified listener paid.
A recording or transcript of any other occasion on which Trump allegedly used the exact quoted words could further test the quotation.

findings.question: For the period relevant to the quoted claim, how much federal income tax did Donald Trump pay or owe, and does the figure of $750 accurately describe it?
findings.summary: The New York Times reported from tax-return data that Trump’s federal income tax was $750 for each of 2016 and 2017. That figure describes income-tax liability for each year, before withholding and prepayments, not necessarily the cash remitted during the year. It does not cover all taxes: Trump also paid other federal taxes, and he or his companies paid foreign taxes.

findings.question: For the relevant tax year or years, how did $750 in federal income tax compare with the federal income tax liabilities of individual taxpayers in the United States?
findings.summary: According to Tax Policy Center modeling reported by Vox, about half of U.S. tax units paid more than $750 in federal individual income tax in both 2016 and 2017. A tax unit can be an individual or a married couple, with dependents, and includes people whose income was too low to require filing. Separately, the Congressional Research Service estimated that 44% of U.S. households would pay no federal income tax in 2016. The comparison therefore applies to many taxpayers, but whether a particular listener paid more cannot be determined without their tax information.

sources.title: Donald Trump paid $750 in income tax in 2017. About half of Americans paid more.
sources.snippet: Mark Mazur, the director of the Tax Policy Center (America’s leading nonpartisan tax think tank) and a former assistant secretary for tax policy at the Treasury Department, told me that according to TPC’s models, about half of American tax units* paid more than $750 in federal income taxes in 2016 and 2017....* A “tax unit” is the Tax Policy Center’s term for “an individual, or a married couple, that files a tax return or would file a tax return if their income were high enough, along with all dependents of that individual or married couple.”

sources.snippet: An estimated 44% of U.S. households will pay no federal income tax in 2016. Some individuals or households do not pay federal income taxes because their income was below the filing threshold.

sources.title: Trump Paid $750 in Federal Income Taxes in 2017. Here’s the Math.
sources.snippet: The small amount of federal income taxes President Trump paid in both 2016 and 2017 — just $750 each year — has become the focus of much attention since it was revealed in a New York Times investigation.

caveats: The roughly half figure is a model estimate for tax units, not a count of individual people or filed returns.
The comparison concerns federal individual income tax, not payroll, state, local, or other taxes.
The 44% estimate uses households, a different population from tax units.

findings.question: What did Donald Trump actually say about being smart and using the tax system when his taxes were raised, and in what context did he say it?
findings.summary: During the September 26, 2016 presidential debate, Hillary Clinton suggested Trump had paid no federal income tax in years covered by records submitted for a casino license. Trump interjected, “That makes me smart.” Neither “Because I’m smart” nor “I know how to game the system” was his wording in that exchange; they paraphrase his remark rather than quote it verbatim. Separately, at an October 3, 2016 rally, Trump said he had legally and “brilliantly” used the tax laws to his benefit.

sources.title: The First Presidential Debate
sources.snippet:
(SOUNDBITE OF 2016 PRESIDENTIAL DEBATE)

CLINTON: Maybe he doesn't want the American people, all of you watching tonight, to know that he's paid nothing in federal taxes because the only years that anybody's ever seen were a couple of years when he had to turn them over to state authorities when he was trying to get a casino license, and they showed he didn't pay any federal income tax. So...

TRUMP: That makes me smart.
